Former President of the African Development Bank, Dr Akinwumi Adesina, has urged President Bola Tinubu and his counterparts in Rwanda and Egypt to provide political leadership for a proposed $50bn investment drive to develop Africa’s space economy. He also proposed the establishment of an Africa Space Future Fund to mobilise investments in the continent’s space industry over the next 10 to 15 years. Adesina identified Tinubu, Rwandan President Paul Kagame and Egyptian President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi as potential founding political anchors of the initiative, citing their countries’ commitments to space development and technological innovation. According to a statement on Wednesday, Adesina made the proposals at the Africa Space Economy, Innovation and Communication Conference 2026 in Abuja. He said, “To provide the political leadership and continental standing this initiative deserves, I propose that three African Presidents provide its founding political anchor: President Bola Ahmed Tinubu of Nigeria, President Paul Kagame of Rwanda, and President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi of Egypt. “Nigeria brings its ambition and growing commitment to space technology. Rwanda brings its experience in technology-driven development and innovation. Egypt brings its established space infrastructure and its role as host of the African Space Agency.” Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Adesina clarified that the $50bn target was not a request for African governments to contribute the amount from their national budgets, but a long-term investment mobilisation plan. He said, “To bridge this gap, I propose the establishment of a 5bn and progressively build the fund’s capacity to mobilise up to $`50bn in cumulative investments over 10 to 15 years. “Let me emphasise that the `$50bn is a long-term investment mobilisation target. It is not a demand for African governments to provide that amount from their national budgets.” He said the fund would bring together governments, sovereign wealth funds, development finance institutions, pension funds, insurance companies, private investors, international partners and the African diaspora. Adesina stressed the need for an independently governed fund with professional investment management, proper due diligence and transparent accountability. He also proposed the Africa Link initiative as a flagship continental programme to expand satellite connectivity and strengthen Africa’s capacity to own and operate its digital infrastructure. According to him, the initiative would begin by aggregating demand, developing shared ground infrastructure and establishing partnerships with satellite operators before progressing to African network operations, technology development, manufacturing and ownership. Adesina urged African countries to move beyond being consumers of technologies developed elsewhere and position themselves as innovators, manufacturers and investors in the global space economy. He said, “Africa must move beyond being a consumer of technologies developed elsewhere. We must become innovators, manufacturers, investors and active participants in the global space economy.” He noted that the global space economy was valued at 1.8tn by 2035, saying Africa needed to increase its investments to benefit from the industry’s growth. He said the continent should aspire to become one of the world’s leading space economies by 2050. The former AfDB president maintained that Africa’s participation in the space economy should go beyond acquiring satellites to developing local capabilities, creating businesses and retaining value within the continent. Africa’s space sector has expanded through the establishment of national space agencies and investments in satellite technology for telecommunications, weather forecasting, agriculture, environmental monitoring and security. However, the continent remains heavily dependent on foreign technology and funding, with limited local capacity in satellite manufacturing and space infrastructure.
